Achilles Tendinopathy — The Calf-to-Heel Connection

Achilles tendon anatomy, midportion and insertional symptoms, evaluation, tailored management and rupture warning signs.

Research behind the infographic

  • Noninsertional disease affects the middle tendon; insertional disease affects its heel attachment. [1]
  • Affected tendon fibers can develop tiny tears, degeneration, swelling and thickening; this is not the same as a complete rupture. [1]
  • Symptoms include morning stiffness, pain along the tendon or heel worsened by activity, and swelling. [1]
  • Assessment starts with history and examination; imaging may be selected and MRI is not always needed for diagnosis. [1]
  • Reducing aggravating activity, supportive footwear and physical therapy including supervised strengthening can help; treatment must be tailored to the individual. [1] [2]
  • Recovery can take months; persistent symptoms should be assessed by a clinician. [1] [2]
  • Sudden severe pain or a pop at the back of the calf or heel may signal rupture and requires urgent medical assessment. [1] [2]

Acute Pancreatitis — An Inflamed Pancreas

Source-backed anatomy, symptoms, causes, urgent warning signs and hospital management of acute pancreatitis.

Research behind the infographic

  • The pancreas lies behind the stomach near the duodenum; it makes insulin and digestive enzymes that normally help digest food in the intestine. [1]
  • Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas; digestive enzymes can damage pancreatic tissue. [1]
  • Gallstones can block the opening of the pancreas; gallstones and heavy alcohol use are common causes, while some medicines and other conditions can also cause it. [2]
  • Symptoms include sudden persistent severe upper abdominal pain that may spread to the back, nausea, vomiting and fever. [2]
  • Sudden severe persistent abdominal pain needs urgent medical evaluation; severe pain spreading to the back, fast heartbeat or difficulty breathing warrants emergency care. [2]
  • Evaluation uses history, examination, blood tests and sometimes imaging such as CT. [2]
  • Hospital treatment includes monitoring, IV fluids and pain relief; treating the cause may include gallstone surgery or alcohol cessation support. Antibiotics are for infection, not a routine cure. [2]
  • Most people recover, but severe illness may cause tissue death or infection and can be life-threatening. [2]
  • Reducing or avoiding alcohol, stopping smoking and following clinician dietary advice may help prevent recurrence. [2]

Multiple Sclerosis — Myelin and Signal Disruption

Central nervous system demyelination, symptoms, diagnosis, management and stroke-related warning signs.

Research behind the infographic

  • Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated disorder affecting the central nervous system: brain and spinal cord; immune attacks damage myelin around axons and may damage axons themselves, disrupting communication. [1] [2]
  • Myelin is the protective coating around nerve fibers; demyelinated lesions can occur in the brain and spinal cord and can be seen with MRI. [1] [2]
  • Symptoms vary by person and lesion location: fatigue, visual problems, numbness or tingling, muscle weakness or stiffness, and balance problems can occur. [1] [2]
  • Some people have relapses and remissions; others experience progressive worsening. The course varies and cannot be predicted from a single illustration. [1] [2]
  • The exact cause is unclear; genetic susceptibility and environmental factors contribute, and smoking and prior Epstein-Barr virus infection are associated with increased risk, not certainty of disease. [1] [2]
  • No single test diagnoses MS: a neurologist combines history and examination with MRI and sometimes spinal fluid or other tests, excluding other causes. [1] [2]
  • There is no current cure. Disease-modifying therapies can reduce relapses and slow progression for appropriate patients; treatment depends on disease type and individual needs. [1] [2]
  • Corticosteroids may speed recovery from a relapse but do not change the long-term course; physiotherapy, tailored exercise, fatigue management and symptom medicines can help. [1] [2]
  • Sudden arm weakness or numbness, sudden vision loss or sudden balance problems can signal stroke and require emergency medical help; do not assume they are MS. [2]
  • MS-like symptoms can have other causes and should be checked by a clinician; general education is not diagnosis. [1] [2]

Urinary Tract Infection — Bladder and Ascending Infection

Source-backed urinary anatomy, bladder infection mechanism, symptoms, risk context, care and urgent warnings.

Research behind the infographic

  • The urinary tract includes two kidneys, two ureters, a bladder and a urethra; kidneys produce urine, ureters carry it to the bladder, the bladder stores it, and the urethra carries it outside. [3]
  • Bacteria, usually from the bowel, can enter through the urethra and multiply in the bladder; an untreated bladder infection can develop into a kidney infection. [1] [2]
  • Burning urination, urgency, frequency, lower abdominal discomfort and sometimes blood in urine are symptoms; smell or dark urine alone does not establish UTI. [1] [2]
  • Catheters, impaired bladder emptying, pregnancy and menopause can increase risk. [2]
  • Clinical assessment uses symptoms and history and may include urine testing; urine testing is not always needed. [1] [2]
  • Antibiotics are often used for bacterial bladder infection; take prescribed treatment as directed. Rest and appropriate fluids may help symptoms, but cranberry products do not treat an established infection. [1] [2]
  • Fever or chills, back pain below the ribs, blood in urine, pregnancy, or rapid worsening warrant urgent medical advice; new confusion, marked drowsiness or difficulty speaking warrant emergency help. [2]
  • Not holding urine, taking time to empty the bladder and drinking appropriate fluids may help urinary health; follow clinician fluid limits when applicable. [2] [3]

Lichens — Two Kingdoms, One Body

How lichens form a fungus-photobiont partnership with a layered thallus, three growth forms and dual reproduction

Research behind the infographic

  • A lichen is a stable symbiotic partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner (photobiont): green algae and/or cyanobacteria. [1] [3]
  • The photobiont photosynthesizes and supplies sugars (carbon) to the fungus; the partnership is thought to be a mutualism. [1] [3]
  • The fungus is the dominant partner and gives the lichen most of its characteristics, including thallus shape and fruiting bodies. [1]
  • About 90% of lichens use a green-algal photobiont; some lichens have both green algae and cyanobacteria. [1] [3]
  • Lichens have no roots, stems, leaves, waxy cuticle or vascular tissue; they absorb water and nutrients from air and rain. [1] [2]
  • The thallus is layered: an outer cortex of tightly packed fungal cells, an algal layer beneath it, and a medulla of loosely packed threadlike fungal filaments. [2]
  • When a lichen is wet, cortex cells become transparent and the algal layer's color shows through; green algae often make a wet lichen bright green. [2]
  • Rhizines are fungal filaments from the medulla that attach the lichen to its surface; they do not move water or nutrients like roots. [2]
  • Some foliose lichens attach by one central holdfast (umbilicate lichens, such as rock tripe). [2]
  • Three main growth forms: crustose (pressed against the surface like a crust), foliose (leafy, with distinct upper and lower sides), fruticose (hair-like, shrubby or cup-like). [2] [3]
  • The fungus produces spores from fruiting bodies; a new fungus must find a compatible photobiont partner. [2]
  • Lichens also reproduce vegetatively: soredia are granules of algae and fungi intertwined for dispersal, isidia are vegetative outgrowths, and fragments can grow into new thalli. [2]
  • By protecting its photobiont, the fungus lets lichens live in dry, sunny places where algae alone could not, recharging with occasional rain. [1]
  • Lichens absorb pollutants such as heavy metals and sulfur from the air, so scientists use them to monitor air quality; old man's beard (Usnea longissima) is an air-pollution indicator. [1] [2]
  • Lichens are not mosses: mosses are plants with leaf-like structures, while lichens are not plants. [1]
